To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of latent tuberculosis infection in a population-based sample of 5–14-year-old children was 1.3% in the Netherlands, and that this prevalence was higher in children of non-western origin.

the risk of progression to active tuberculosis was higher in patients with a recent history of pulmonary tuberculosis and in patients with HIV co-infection, and that the risk was lower in patients with an underlying condition that predisposed to tuberculosis and in older patients.

(i) a single interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) test is a useful tool for the diagnosis of LTBI, and that (ii) IGRA testing should not be performed as the sole criterion for the decision to initiate treatment for latent tuberculosis infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of tuberculosis in the context of HIV/AIDS.
the development and evaluation of diagnostic and preventive measures for tuberculosis and other infectious diseases.
the development of new diagnostic tools, and the evaluation of new diagnostic strategies for the detection and management of latent tuberculosis infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the WHO recommendations for screening and treatment of LTBI are based on a very limited evidence-base and are therefore not justified.
the evidence for screening and treatment of LTBI to reduce active TB in the general population is insufficient.
screening for LTBI in high-income countries is a cost-effective measure for the prevention of active tuberculosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of progression to tuberculosis is increased in the first 2 years after infection, and that the risk is highest in children and young adults [2].
we have shown that it is possible to identify a group of patients with LTBI, and that treatment is effective in reducing the risk of active disease in this group.
the guidelines are based on limited evidence, and that the recommendations for screening are often not supported by evidence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of LTBI in the general population is low, and that the benefits of LTBI screening are therefore limited.
the prevalence of LTBI is high among healthcare workers, and that the risk of active tuberculosis among healthcare workers with LTBI is higher than in the general population.
LTBI screening should not be done routinely in the general population, because the benefit of screening is too small compared to the harm.
